A.explanation: Current of $10 \text{ A}$ loses $10 \text{ V}$ in the two $0.50 \text{ } \Omega$ wires, leaving $230 \text{ V}$ and about $2.3 \text{ kW}$ for the kettle.

B.explanation: Power loss of $0.1 \text{ kW}$ is allowed for but only $5 \text{ V}$ for one wire is subtracted, giving $235 \text{ V}$ instead of the drop in both wires.

C.explanation: The p.d. of $230 \text{ V}$ allows for both wire drops but $2.4 \text{ kW}$ wrongly assumes no power is lost as heat in the wires.

D.explanation: Both values ignore one wire: $2.4 \text{ kW}$ assumes no loss and $235 \text{ V}$ subtracts only one $5 \text{ V}$ drop.

hints: Find the current leaving the $240 \text{ V}$, $2.4 \text{ kW}$ supply using $P = VI$, since this same current flows through both $0.50 \text{ } \Omega$ wires and the kettle.
Use $V = IR$ for one $0.50 \text{ } \Omega$ wire and remember there are two wires in series, so the total lost p.d. is twice the drop in one wire.
Subtract the total wire drop from $240 \text{ V}$ to get the kettle p.d., then subtract the $I^2R$ heating loss in both wires from $2.4 \text{ kW}$ to get the kettle power.
walkthrough: Calculate the circuit current from the supply rating: $I = P/V = 2400/240 = 10 \text{ A}$. This current flows through each $0.50 \text{ } \Omega$ connecting wire and the kettle in series.
Calculate the p.d. lost across one wire: $V_{wire} = IR = 10 \times 0.50 = 5.0 \text{ V}$. With two wires the total lost p.d. is $2 \times 5.0 = 10 \text{ V}$.
Find the p.d. left across the kettle: $V_{kettle} = 240 - 10 = 230 \text{ V}$. This rules out the $235 \text{ V}$ options which only subtract one wire.
Find the power wasted in the wires: $P_{loss} = 2 \times I^2R = 2 \times 10^2 \times 0.50 = 100 \text{ W} = 0.10 \text{ kW}$.
Find the power delivered to the kettle: $P_{kettle} = 2.4 - 0.10 = 2.3 \text{ kW}$ to two significant figures. The $2.3 \text{ kW}$ and $230 \text{ V}$ combination is option A.
